name: auth
purpose: Owns everything about proving who a caller is: registration, email verification, login, multi-factor authentication, token issuance and rotation, session lifecycle, password reset, and OAuth sign-in. It answers "who is this?" and nothing else.
context: Authentication is deliberately separated from `user` (profile data) and `rbac` (what the caller may do). Keeping the three apart means a change to profile fields cannot break login, and a change to permissions cannot break token issuance.
businessPurpose: Learners must be able to create an account and return to it safely from any device. Administrators must be held to a higher standard (mandatory MFA) because they can see and change everyone's data. Every authentication event must be reconstructable after the fact.
responsibilities: Registration and email verification by one-time code (OTP)
The generic challenge subsystem: issue, resend, verify and burn short-lived codes for any purpose
Password hashing (Argon2id), verification, and policy enforcement including breached-password checks
Access token (JWT, 15 min) issuance and validation
Refresh token issuance, **sliding** rotation, reuse detection and family revocation
Persistent sign-in: trusted devices, sliding idle window, absolute re-authentication cap
Session records: creation, listing, revocation (by the user and by an admin)
TOTP multi-factor enrolment, verification and recovery codes
Password reset and change flows
Google OAuth sign-in (authorization code + PKCE) and account linking by verified email only
Brute-force protection: per-IP, per-account and per-challenge lockout
Emitting security events for the audit trail
notResponsibilities: Profile data, preferences, avatars — that is `user`
What a caller is allowed to do — that is `rbac`
Storing the audit log — it emits events, `audit` persists them
Sending the emails — it asks `platform/mailer` to
Rate limiting infrastructure — it uses `platform/cache`

tables.name: credentials
tables.notes: `user_id` UNIQUE, `password_hash`, `algo_params`, `updated_at`. Never selected in a list query.

tables.name: sessions
tables.notes: `user_id`, `device_label`, `ip_hash`, `user_agent_hash`, `last_seen_at`, `revoked_at`

tables.name: refresh_tokens
tables.notes: `token_hash` (SHA-256) UNIQUE, `family_id`, `session_id`, `used_at`, `expires_at`. Reuse of a used row revokes the whole family.

tables.name: mfa_secrets
tables.notes: Seed encrypted with a KEK; recovery codes stored hashed and single-use

tables.name: auth_challenges
tables.purpose: Short-lived one-time codes for every purpose
tables.notes: `id` (the challenge handle returned to the client), `purpose` enum (`verify_email`, `login_otp`, `password_reset`, `link_oauth`), `subject_hash`, `code_hash` (HMAC-SHA256 with a server key), `attempts`, `max_attempts`, `expires_at`, `consumed_at`. 10-minute TTL, single use.

tables.name: trusted_devices
tables.purpose: Devices the learner chose to stay signed in on
tables.notes: `user_id`, `device_id` (client-generated, stored hashed), `label`, `idle_window`, `absolute_expires_at`, `last_seen_at`, `revoked_at`

tables.name: login_attempts
tables.notes: `email_hash`, `ip_hash`, `success`, `failure_reason`, `created_at`; indexed for lockout-window lookups

tables.name: login_lockouts
tables.notes: One row per `account` or `ip` HMAC; guarded upsert advances `lockout_level` and `locked_until` atomically

tables.name: oauth_identities
tables.notes: `provider`, `subject`, `email_hash`, `linked_at`, UNIQUE(provider, subject)

tables.name: oauth_states
tables.notes: `state` UNIQUE, `nonce`, `pkce_verifier_hash`, `redirect_to`, `expires_at`. 10-minute TTL, single use — this is the CSRF defence for the OAuth flow.

indexes: `uq_refresh_tokens_hash` — unique on `token_hash`, the lookup path on every refresh
`idx_refresh_tokens_family` — used to revoke a whole family in one statement
`login_lockouts_pkey` — one lockout state per scope and subject hash

endpoints.purpose: Create an account and issue a `verify_email` OTP challenge
endpoints.notes: Returns a `challenge_id`; the 6-digit code goes to the email. The account cannot sign in until verified.

endpoints.purpose: Submit the OTP code for a challenge
endpoints.notes: Generic across every purpose. Consumes the challenge on success; burns it after `max_attempts`.

endpoints.purpose: Resend the code for a challenge
endpoints.notes: 60-second cooldown, 3 issuances per subject per hour. Issues a new code and resets attempts; the challenge id is unchanged.
Accepts `remember_device` and an optional client `device_id`. Response timing is equalised between 'unknown email' and 'wrong password'; token issuance arrives in P2.4.

endpoints.purpose: Begin Google sign-in; returns the authorization URL
endpoints.notes: Generates `state`, `nonce` and a PKCE challenge, stored server-side with a 10-minute TTL

endpoints.purpose: Complete a login that required a second factor
Rotate the refresh token and issue a new access token
endpoints.notes: Reuse of an already-used token revokes the entire family and raises a security event

endpoints.purpose: Revoke the current session and refresh family

endpoints.notes: Always returns 202 regardless of whether the email exists

endpoints.purpose: Consume a reset token and set a new password
endpoints.notes: Revokes all sessions on success

endpoints.purpose: Change the password while signed in
Begin TOTP enrolment; returns a provisioning URI and recovery codes
Complete Google sign-in: verify state, exchange the code, validate the ID token, link or create the account
Link a Google identity to the signed-in account

endpoints.notes: Refused if it would leave the account with no way to sign in

endpoints.purpose: List trusted devices with their idle and absolute expiry
Untrust a device, revoking its refresh family
Admin revokes all sessions for a user

contract.name: auth.TokenVerifier
contract.purpose: Validate an access token and return the actor — used by the HTTP middleware

contract.name: auth.SessionRevoker
contract.purpose: `RevokeAll(ctx, userID) (int, error)` — used by `admin` on suspension and by `user` on account deletion. Published and unconsumed until those modules exist

contract.name: auth.Actor
contract.purpose: `{UserID, SessionID, Role, TokenID}` — placed in the request context

contract.name: auth.SecurityEvent
contract.purpose: Published when something needs investigating — `refresh_reuse` (a single-use credential presented twice) and `oauth_state_invalid` (a Google callback carrying a state this server did not issue, or already spent)

consumes.name: user.deletion_requested
consumes.reason: Revoke all sessions and credentials immediately. **Not yet subscribed** — `contract.SessionRevoker.RevokeAll` is built and tested but nothing calls it. P3.3 adds the subscription

dependsWhy.user: Create the user record on registration; read status (active/suspended) on login
dependsWhy.rbac: Attach the caller's role to the issued token
dependsWhy.mailer: Send verification, reset and new-device emails
dependsWhy.cache: Lockout counters, rate limits, token denylist

usedByWhy.admin: Revoke sessions, force password reset, inspect login history

rules: A password must be at least 12 characters and must not appear in the breached-password corpus.
Login responses for an unknown email and a wrong password are indistinguishable in content and comparable in timing.
An access token is valid for 15 minutes and carries no personal data beyond the user ID.
A refresh token is single-use. Presenting a used token revokes every token in its family and raises a `refresh_reuse` security event.
Changing or resetting a password revokes all sessions except, optionally, the current one.
Email verification is required before any AI-consuming feature may be used.
MFA is mandatory for accounts holding the `admin` role; a promotion to admin forces enrolment on next login.
Five failed attempts within 15 minutes lock the account for an exponentially increasing period, tracked per account and per IP independently.
A suspended user's tokens stop working within one access-token lifetime (15 min); their sessions are revoked immediately on suspension.

Every one-time code is 6 digits, single-use, allows at most 5 verification attempts, and is stored only as an HMAC — never in plaintext, never in a log. It expires in 10 minutes unless its purpose sets otherwise; `password_reset` gets 30, because a reset email can sit unread in a way a signup code typed on the next screen cannot.
A code is worthless without its `challenge_id`. The client receives the id; the code goes to the email. Guessing a code alone gets an attacker nothing.
Exceeding `max_attempts` burns the challenge permanently. A new one must be requested — the code is not simply retried.
Resend has a 60-second cooldown and a cap of 3 issuances per subject per hour. Resending replaces the code and resets attempts; it does not extend the absolute expiry.

Challenge issuance never reveals whether an account exists. `POST /auth/register` on an existing verified email returns the same shape as a fresh registration and sends a 'someone tried to register with your address' email instead.
Google sign-in links to an existing account **only** when Google asserts `email_verified: true` and the email matches a verified local account. An unverified Google email is refused outright.

If a Google email matches an existing account that is **not** yet verified, no automatic link occurs — the learner must complete an OTP challenge on that address first. Otherwise anyone who can register an unverified address could hijack it via a Google account.
The OAuth `state` is server-side, single-use and 10-minute-lived, and PKCE is mandatory even though we hold a client secret.
Google's ID token is verified against Google's JWKS: signature, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, and the `nonce` we issued. A token that fails any check is rejected without a partial account being created.
An account signed in via Google skips email verification — Google has already performed it.
Unlinking the last sign-in method is refused; the account must always retain at least one way in.
Refresh tokens are **sliding**: each rotation issues a new token with a fresh idle window, so an active learner never signs in again.
Every session carries an **absolute** expiry independent of activity. When it passes, full re-authentication is required regardless of how recently the learner was active.
Idle windows: 30 days by default, 90 days on a device the learner explicitly chose to trust. Absolute cap: 180 days. Admin accounts get neither extension — 12-hour idle, 7-day absolute.
Trusting a device is an explicit opt-in, is listed in the account's device list, and can be revoked from any other device.
A password change, a password reset, or an admin suspension revokes every trusted device and every refresh family.
The system never reveals whether an email address is registered — `forgot-password` always returns 202.

validation.rule: RFC 5322, normalised to lowercase, max 254 chars, MX-checkable domain
≥ 12 chars, not in the breach corpus, not equal to the email local part
6 digits, ±1 time step tolerance, each code usable once

cache.invalidation: Natural expiry — catches distributed guessing across challenges
Respect Google's Cache-Control; never fetch per request

Code older than 10 minutes
Challenge burned; request a new one

security: Access tokens live in browser memory only — never `localStorage`, never a non-HttpOnly cookie.
Refresh tokens are `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/api/v1/auth`.
Password comparison is constant-time; Argon2id parameters are stored in the hash so they can be raised without a migration.
Every authentication failure is logged with `email_hash`, never the address.
Admin session revocation is audited with the acting admin's ID.
The JWT signing key supports two active keys so rotation does not sign everyone out.
OTP codes are stored as `HMAC-SHA256(code, server_key)`, compared in constant time, and never appear in a response, a log, a span attribute or a fixture.
The OAuth `state` and PKCE verifier live server-side and are single-use; the client never holds anything that alone completes a sign-in.
Google's JWKS is cached with its own `Cache-Control` and refreshed on an unknown `kid` — never fetched per request, and never skipped.
A longer idle window is a larger stolen-cookie window. It is bounded by the absolute expiry, revocable per device, and refused entirely for admin accounts.
Every OAuth failure branch (bad state, unverified email, account conflict) raises a security event — these are the signals an account-takeover attempt produces.
rateLimits: `/auth/login`, `/auth/register`, `/auth/forgot-password`: 5/min per IP **and** per account, with exponential lockout

flows.title: Registration with OTP verification
flows.description: The account, the credential and the challenge are created in one transaction; the email is dispatched through the outbox so a code can never be sent for a rolled-back registration. The learner stays on the same screen and types the code — no context switch to a second browser.
flows.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor U as User
    participant A as auth
    participant US as user (contract)
    participant D as PostgreSQL
    participant M as mailer

    U->>A: POST /auth/register { email, password }
    A->>A: validate email + password policy + breach corpus
    A->>D: BEGIN
    A->>US: CreateUser(email, locale)
    US->>D: INSERT core.users (status=pending_verification)
    A->>D: INSERT core.credentials (argon2id)
    A->>D: INSERT auth_challenges (purpose=verify_email, code_hash=HMAC(code), attempts=0, ttl=10m)
    A->>D: INSERT outbox(send verify_email code)
    A->>D: COMMIT
    A-->>U: 201 { challenge_id, expires_at, resend_after }
    Note over D,M: outbox → mailer job — never a direct call
    M->>U: email containing the 6-digit code

    loop up to 5 attempts
        U->>A: POST /auth/challenges/{id}/verify { code }
        A->>D: load challenge; check expiry and attempts
        A->>A: constant-time compare against code_hash
        alt wrong
            A->>D: attempts += 1
            A-->>U: 401 OTP_INVALID { attempts_remaining }
        else attempts exhausted
            A->>D: burn challenge
            A-->>U: 429 OTP_ATTEMPTS_EXCEEDED
        else correct
            A->>D: BEGIN; consume challenge; users.status = active
            A->>D: INSERT outbox(user.registered); COMMIT
            A-->>U: 200 { access_token } + refresh cookie
        end
    end

flows.title: Google sign-in with account linking
flows.description: The dangerous branch is the one in the middle: a Google email that matches an **unverified** local account. Auto-linking there is the classic account-takeover path, so it is refused.
flows.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor U as User
    participant W as SPA
    participant A as auth
    participant G as Google
    participant D as PostgreSQL

    U->>W: tap 'Continue with Google'
    W->>A: GET /auth/oauth/google/start
    A->>D: INSERT oauth_states (state, nonce, pkce_verifier_hash, ttl=10m)
    A-->>W: { authorization_url }
    W->>G: redirect
    U->>G: consent
    G->>W: redirect back with code + state
    W->>A: POST /auth/oauth/google/callback { code, state }
    A->>D: load + consume state (single use)
    alt missing, reused or expired
        A-->>W: 400 OAUTH_STATE_INVALID + security event
    end
    A->>G: exchange code (with PKCE verifier)
    G-->>A: id_token + access_token
    A->>G: fetch JWKS; verify signature, iss, aud, exp, nonce
    alt email_verified is false
        A-->>W: 403 OAUTH_EMAIL_UNVERIFIED
    end
    A->>D: look up oauth_identities by (google, sub)
    alt identity known
        A->>A: sign in
    else email matches a VERIFIED local account
        A->>D: INSERT oauth_identities (link)
        A->>A: sign in
    else email matches an UNVERIFIED local account
        A-->>W: 409 OAUTH_ACCOUNT_CONFLICT — verify by OTP first
    else no local account
        A->>D: create user (status=active, email already verified by Google)
        A->>A: sign in
    end
    A-->>W: 200 { access_token } + refresh cookie

flows.title: Staying signed in — sliding window with an absolute cap
flows.description: This is what 'log in once' actually means in a design that can still revoke a stolen credential. The idle window moves forward on every use; the absolute expiry does not.
flows.mermaid:
flowchart TD A[Login with remember_device = true] --> B[create session:
idle_window = 90d
absolute_expires_at = now + 180d] B --> C[refresh token issued, expires = now + idle_window] C --> D{App opened} D --> E{now > absolute_expires_at?} E -->|yes| F[401 SESSION_ABSOLUTE_EXPIRED
full re-authentication] E -->|no| G{refresh token expired?} G -->|yes| H[401 — idle too long, sign in again] G -->|no| I[rotate: new token, expires = now + idle_window] I --> J[access token issued
learner never saw a login screen] J --> D K[Password change / reset /
admin suspend / device untrusted] --> L[revoke every family
+ every trusted device] L --> F

flows.title: Refresh rotation with reuse detection
flows.description: The single most security-critical flow in the system. A stolen refresh token is detectable because the legitimate client will eventually present the same token the attacker already used.
flows.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant A as auth
    participant D as PostgreSQL
    participant AU as audit

    C->>A: POST /auth/refresh (cookie)
    A->>D: SELECT refresh_tokens WHERE token_hash = $1
    alt not found
        A-->>C: 401 TOKEN_INVALID
    else used_at IS NOT NULL
        A->>D: UPDATE refresh_tokens SET revoked_at = now() WHERE family_id = $f
        A->>D: UPDATE sessions SET revoked_at = now() WHERE id = $s
        A->>AU: security_event(refresh_reuse, severity=high)
        A-->>C: 401 SESSION_REVOKED
    else valid
        A->>D: BEGIN
        A->>D: UPDATE refresh_tokens SET used_at = now() WHERE id = $1
        A->>D: INSERT refresh_tokens (new hash, same family_id)
        A->>D: UPDATE sessions SET last_seen_at = now()
        A->>D: COMMIT
        A-->>C: 200 { access_token } + Set-Cookie
    end

stateMachine.description: Account lifecycle. Note that `suspended` is reversible and `deleted` is not — deletion runs through a 30-day grace period owned by `user`.
stateMachine.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> PendingVerification: register
    PendingVerification --> Active: verify email
    PendingVerification --> [*]: expire after 7 days
    Active --> Locked: too many failed attempts
    Locked --> Active: lockout expires or admin unlocks
    Active --> Suspended: admin suspends
    Suspended --> Active: admin reinstates
    Active --> PendingDeletion: user requests deletion
    Suspended --> PendingDeletion: user requests deletion
    PendingDeletion --> Active: user cancels within 30 days
    PendingDeletion --> [*]: anonymised after 30 days

failures.behaviour: Account is created; the email is retried with backoff; the user can request a resend
Lockout counters fall back to a database query; login still works, with a warn log
Fail open with a warn log — a weak password is worse than a blocked registration, but an outage must not block signups
60-second leeway on `exp`/`nbf`; NTP is a host requirement

tasks.title: Add a new OAuth provider
steps: Add the provider config keys to `shared/config` and `.env.example`.
Implement the provider adapter in `service/oauth/<provider>.go` behind the existing `oauthProvider` interface.
Register it in `module.go`'s provider map.
Add the callback path to `api/openapi/openapi.yaml` (it is parameterised, so usually no change).
Add a fixture-backed unit test and an integration test with a stubbed token endpoint.
Update §4 and §9 of this AGENT.md and `docs/security/authentication.md`.

tasks.title: Change token lifetimes
steps: Change `ACCESS_TTL` / `REFRESH_TTL` in config — never hard-code a duration.
Check the frontend's silent-refresh margin still fits (it refreshes at 80 % of the access TTL).
Update the denylist TTL, which must be ≥ the access TTL.
Update `docs/deployment/configuration.md` and this file §9.

tasks.title: Add a new security event kind
steps: Add the kind to `contract/events.go` with a severity.
Publish it from the relevant service method through the outbox.
Confirm `audit` persists it (it consumes the generic event, so usually no change there).
Add an alert rule if the event should page someone, plus a runbook.

limitations: MFA is TOTP only. WebAuthn/passkeys are the obvious next step but are not in Phase 1.

A 6-digit OTP is 10^6 of entropy. Five attempts per challenge plus per-subject and per-IP issuance limits keep the per-challenge guess probability at 5 in a million, but a distributed guessing campaign across many challenges still needs the global rate limiter to catch it — that limiter is load-bearing, not decorative.
OTP delivery depends on email latency. A learner on a slow provider may wait; the resend cooldown is deliberately short (60 s) to compensate.
Google is the only social provider. Apple is deferred until an iOS app exists, where the App Store requires it.

Device identity is a client-generated `device_id` in local storage plus a coarse fingerprint. Clearing browser storage looks like a new device, which is the correct failure direction but does mean a re-login.
The breached-password check requires an outbound call; the offline Bloom-filter fallback is not yet built.
OAuth account linking requires a verified email match; providers that do not assert verification are not supported.
Session geolocation is IP-country only, from a local database — it is indicative, not evidence.
conventions: Never log an email address. Log `user_id`, or `email_hash` when there is no user yet.
Every timing-sensitive comparison uses `crypto/subtle` or the argon2id verifier.
Token strings never appear in a struct that has a `String()` or is ever logged — wrap them in `shared/secret.Redacted[string]`.
All token TTLs come from config; a literal duration in this module is a review failure.
testFocus: Refresh reuse detection: reusing a rotated token must revoke the whole family
Login timing: unknown email and wrong password must not be distinguishable
Lockout: counters per account and per IP behave independently and expire correctly
Password change and reset revoke sessions
MFA: replayed code rejected; recovery code single-use; clock-skew tolerance
Suspended user cannot refresh, and existing access tokens stop working within one TTL
OTP: single-use, 10-minute expiry, exactly 5 attempts then burned, constant-time comparison
OTP: the code is never in the API response, never in a log, never in a span attribute
OTP: resend cooldown and hourly cap; resend replaces the code but does not extend the absolute expiry
OTP: a code from challenge A does not verify challenge B
OAuth: forged, reused and expired `state` all rejected; each raises a security event
OAuth: an ID token failing signature, `iss`, `aud`, `exp` or `nonce` creates no account and no partial state
OAuth: unverified Google email refused; match against an unverified local account refused
OAuth: unlinking the only sign-in method refused
Sliding refresh: rotation moves the idle window forward but never past the absolute expiry
Absolute expiry forces re-authentication even for a continuously active session
Admin accounts do not receive the extended idle window
Password change, reset and suspension all revoke every trusted device
testEdges: Two concurrent refreshes with the same valid token — exactly one must succeed
Registration with an email that differs only in case or by a Unicode homoglyph
A refresh presented one millisecond after expiry
Password reset requested twice — the first token must be invalidated
Login during an in-progress password change

decisions.question: JWT or opaque access tokens?
decisions.choice: JWT (HS256 now, EdDSA when services split)
decisions.why: Stateless validation keeps the middleware free of a database round trip on every request; the 15-minute lifetime bounds the revocation window, and the denylist covers explicit logout

decisions.question: Where does the refresh token live?
decisions.why: Not reachable by JavaScript, so an XSS cannot steal it; the narrow path limits CSRF surface to one endpoint, which also carries a double-submit token

decisions.question: Argon2id or bcrypt?
decisions.why: OWASP's first recommendation; memory-hardness resists GPU cracking; parameters embedded in the hash allow raising cost without a migration

decisions.question: Store sessions in Redis or Postgres?
decisions.why: Sessions are durable state a user can audit and an admin can revoke; Redis is a 5-minute read cache, not the source of truth

decisions.question: Verification by emailed link or by OTP code?
decisions.why: A majority of learners open email on a phone. A link launches a second browser context with no session, which breaks the flow and loses the registration. A 6-digit code is typed into the tab already open. See ADR-0021

decisions.question: One challenge table or a table per purpose?
decisions.why: Rate limiting, attempt capping, hashing, expiry and burning are identical across purposes. Three copies would mean three places to get constant-time comparison wrong

decisions.question: How is 'stay signed in' implemented?
decisions.choice: Sliding idle window + absolute cap, not a long-lived token
decisions.why: An active learner is never signed out, which is the actual requirement, while every credential still has a bounded lifetime and a revocation path. See ADR-0022

decisions.question: Which social providers in Phase 1?
decisions.why: It covers the overwhelming majority of the target market. Apple can wait until there is an iOS app, where it becomes a store requirement

decisions.question: What happens when a Google email matches an unverified local account?
decisions.choice: Refuse and require OTP verification of that address first
decisions.why: Auto-linking would let anyone who registers an address they do not own capture it later via Google. This is the subtle account-takeover path in every social login integration

doNot: Do not put the access token in `localStorage` or a readable cookie.
Do not add profile fields here — they belong to `user`.
Do not check permissions here — that is `rbac`. This module only proves identity.
Do not return different messages or noticeably different timings for unknown-email and wrong-password.
Do not extend the access-token lifetime to avoid refresh complexity.
Do not log tokens, password hashes, email addresses, TOTP seeds, or OTP codes — not even at debug level, not even in a test fixture.
Do not implement 'stay signed in' as a token with no expiry. Use the sliding idle window plus the absolute cap; an immortal credential cannot be reasoned about or revoked reliably.
Do not put the OTP code in the API response, in a URL, or in a push notification. It goes to the email channel and nowhere else — otherwise it verifies nothing.
Do not compare an OTP with `==`. Use a constant-time comparison against the stored HMAC.
Do not auto-link a Google identity to an unverified local account.
Do not trust anything in Google's ID token before verifying its signature against the JWKS, plus `iss`, `aud`, `exp` and the `nonce` we issued.
Do not reuse an OAuth `state` value, and do not accept one that did not come from our own store.
Do not skip PKCE because we are a confidential client — it costs nothing and blocks code interception on mobile browsers.

name: user
purpose: Owns the user record and everything descriptive about a person: profile, preferences, locale, timezone, avatar, learning goals, and the account lifecycle including export and deletion. It is the canonical source of `core.users`, which every other module references by ID.
businessPurpose: A learner's experience is personalised by locale, level and goals. A user must be able to see, correct, export and delete everything we hold about them — both because it is right and because privacy regulation requires it.
responsibilities: The `core.users` record: identity, status, timestamps
Profile: display name, avatar, country, timezone, locale, date of birth (for the age gate)
Preferences: notification settings, daily goal, UI theme, AI processing opt-out
Learning profile: self-declared level, goals, target exam, study reminders
Account status transitions: active, suspended, pending deletion
Data export (async) and erasure (30-day grace, then anonymisation)
Avatar upload coordination through `platform/storage`
notResponsibilities: Passwords, sessions, tokens — that is `auth`
Roles and permissions — that is `rbac`
Learning progress and statistics — that is `learning`
Subscription state — that is `subscription`

tables.name: users
tables.notes: `email` (citext, UNIQUE), `status`, `email_verified_at`, `created_at`. **The one table other schemas may FK to** (ADR-0004)

tables.name: profiles
tables.notes: 1:1 with users; display name, avatar asset ID, country, timezone

tables.name: user_preferences
tables.notes: Locale, theme, daily goal, notification channels, quiet hours, `ai_processing_opt_out`

tables.name: learning_profiles
tables.notes: Declared level, target level, target exam, weekly minutes goal, motivations

tables.name: user_deletion_requests
tables.notes: `requested_at`, `execute_after`, `cancelled_at`, `completed_at`

tables.name: user_exports
tables.notes: `status`, `object_key`, `expires_at`

endpoints.purpose: Get a presigned URL for an avatar upload
Get status of a data export request
Get status of an account deletion request

contract.name: user.Reader
contract.purpose: `GetByID`, `GetManyByIDs`, `Exists` — batched to avoid N+1 across modules

contract.name: user.Summary
contract.purpose: `{ID, DisplayName, AvatarURL, Locale, Timezone, Status}` — the shape other modules render

contract.name: user.DeletionRequested
contract.purpose: Every module holding personal data reacts to this

publishes.name: user.deleted
publishes.payload: `{user_id}` — modules must purge or anonymise their data

consumes.name: subscription.activated
consumes.reason: Cache the entitlement tier on the profile for fast reads

rules: `core.users.email` is unique, case-insensitive (citext), and immutable after verification — changing it is a separate verified flow, not a profile edit.
A display name is 1–50 characters, must not impersonate staff (a reserved-word list), and is moderated on report.
Timezone must be a valid IANA name; all stored timestamps remain UTC.
Date of birth is used only for the age gate; users under 16 require a guardian email and receive no marketing.
Deletion is a 30-day grace period: the account is unusable immediately, cancellable by the user, and irreversible afterwards.
On execution, PII is hard-deleted and learning statistics are anonymised to a synthetic ID so aggregate analytics remain valid.
An export is produced asynchronously and delivered as a signed link valid for 24 hours; the artefact is deleted after 7 days.
Suspending a user revokes their sessions immediately via `auth`'s contract.
Setting `ai_processing_opt_out` disables AI grading only; deterministic exercises continue to work.

errors.meaning: Reserved or moderated name
e.g. cancelling a deletion that already executed
One export at a time
Under-16 account without guardian consent

security: Only the account owner and an admin with `user.read` may read a profile; every query filters by actor.
Admin reads of personal data are audited with the acting admin's ID.
Export artefacts live in a private bucket and are reachable only through a short-lived presigned URL.
Avatars are size- and type-limited, stripped of EXIF, and re-encoded before being made public.

flows.title: Account deletion
flows.description: Deletion fans out to every module holding personal data. Each module is responsible for its own erasure, driven by an event rather than a central script — that is what keeps the boundary intact.
flows.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor U as User
    participant US as user
    participant A as auth
    participant J as job
    participant M as all modules

    U->>US: DELETE /me
    US->>US: INSERT deletion_request (execute_after = now + 30d)
    US->>US: users.status = pending_deletion
    US->>A: RevokeAllSessions(user_id)
    US->>US: publish user.deletion_requested
    US-->>U: 202 { execute_after }

    alt user cancels within 30 days
        U->>US: POST /me/deletion/cancel
        US->>US: status = active; cancel request
    else grace elapses
        J->>US: scheduled job picks up due requests
        US->>US: anonymise profile, hard-delete PII
        US->>M: publish user.deleted
        M->>M: each module purges or anonymises its own data
        US->>US: mark completed
    end

stateMachine.description: Account status. `auth` reads this on every login; a non-active status blocks authentication.
stateMachine.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> PendingVerification
    PendingVerification --> Active: email verified
    Active --> Suspended: admin action
    Suspended --> Active: admin reinstates
    Active --> PendingDeletion: user request
    Suspended --> PendingDeletion: user request
    PendingDeletion --> Active: cancelled within 30 days
    PendingDeletion --> Anonymised: grace elapsed
    Anonymised --> [*]

failures.failure: A module fails to purge on `user.deleted`
failures.detection: Erasure completeness job compares expected vs actual
failures.behaviour: Retries, then raises an alert — an incomplete erasure is a compliance incident

failures.failure: Export job exceeds its timeout on a very large account
failures.behaviour: Chunked export with resumable state; user notified when ready

tasks.title: Add a profile field
steps: Decide which table it belongs to: identity (`users`), descriptive (`profiles`), settings (`user_preferences`), or learning context (`learning_profiles`). Do **not** add it to `users`.
Write the migration in `db/migrations/user/`.
Add it to the sqlc query and the domain struct.
Add it to `contract/dto.go` only if another module needs it.
Update `openapi.yaml` and the frontend types via `make gen`.
Add validation, and a test for the boundary values.
Update this AGENT.md §5 and the front-matter `tables:` list.

tasks.title: Add a module that stores personal data
steps: Subscribe to `user.deletion_requested` and `user.deleted` in that module.
Implement idempotent purge or anonymisation.
Add the module to the erasure completeness check.
Document what it holds in `docs/security/data-inventory.md`.

limitations: Email change is not implemented in Phase 1 — it requires a re-verification flow.
Avatar moderation is manual and report-driven; there is no automated image classification.
The export format is a ZIP of JSON and media; there is no interoperable standard we target.
testFocus: Deletion grace period: cancellable before, irreversible after
Anonymisation preserves aggregate statistics while removing PII
Every other module's purge handler is idempotent
Timezone and locale validation, including odd IANA names
Age gate boundaries around the 16th birthday
Admin cannot read a profile without `user.read`, and the read is audited

decisions.question: One `users` table or split identity and profile?
decisions.why: `users` is referenced by every schema; keeping it narrow and stable means profile churn never touches a table with a dozen inbound foreign keys

decisions.question: Hard delete or anonymise?
decisions.why: Satisfies erasure while keeping historical aggregates truthful — deleting the rows outright would silently rewrite past reports

decisions.question: Who owns cross-module erasure?
decisions.choice: Each module, driven by an event
decisions.why: A central deletion script would need to know every module's schema, which is exactly the coupling the architecture exists to prevent

openQuestions: Do we need a verified email-change flow in Phase 2, or is support-assisted change acceptable?

items: `users`, `profiles`, `user_preferences` tables and CRUD
`GET/PATCH /me` and preferences endpoints
Avatar upload via presigned URL, with EXIF stripping
Admin user list, search, suspend, reinstate — all audited
Deletion request with 30-day grace and cancellation
Export job producing a signed link
`user.deleted` fan-out with an erasure completeness check

doNot: Do not add columns to `core.users` — use `profiles`, `user_preferences`, or your own module's table.
Do not read another module's tables to build a profile response; call their contract.
Do not expose `email` in any response other than the owner's own `/me`.
Do not implement deletion as a cascade of `DELETE` statements from this module — publish the event.

name: rbac
purpose: Answers "may this actor do this?". Holds roles, named permissions, and the mapping between them, and provides the guard used by every service method. There are exactly two roles — `admin` and `user` — but permissions are named so that adding a role later is a data change, not a code change.
businessPurpose: Administrators can see and change everything; learners can see and change only their own work. Making that boundary explicit and testable is what prevents the single most common and most damaging class of web vulnerability.
responsibilities: Role definitions and role assignment to users
The permission catalogue (named capabilities)
Role→permission mapping
The `Require(ctx, permission)` guard used by service methods
The route-group middleware for `/admin/*`
Cached permission resolution
notResponsibilities: Proving identity — that is `auth`
Ownership checks (`WHERE user_id = actor`) — those live in each module's queries, because only that module knows what ownership means for its data
Audit logging of denied attempts — it emits, `audit` persists

tables.name: roles
tables.notes: Seeded with exactly `admin` and `user`; adding one is a migration plus a decision

tables.name: permissions
tables.notes: `name` UNIQUE, e.g. `content.publish`; `description` is shown in the admin UI

tables.name: role_permissions
tables.notes: Composite PK (role_id, permission_id)

tables.name: user_roles
tables.notes: Composite PK (user_id, role_id); `granted_by`, `granted_at`

endpoints.purpose: The caller's effective permissions — the frontend uses this to hide unavailable actions
endpoints.notes: Hiding a control is UX, not security; the server still enforces every call

contract.name: rbac.Authorizer
contract.purpose: `Require(ctx, permission) error` and `Can(ctx, permission) bool` — the guard every service uses

contract.name: rbac.RoleReader
contract.purpose: `RolesOf(ctx, userID)` — used by `auth` when minting a token

contract.name: rbac.Perm*
contract.purpose: Typed permission constants; a permission is never a bare string at a call site

dependsWhy.cache: Permission sets are read on nearly every request
dependsWhy.audit: Role changes and denials are security-relevant

rules: Deny by default: an operation with no declared permission is refused, not allowed.
Exactly two roles exist. Introducing a third requires an ADR — it changes the product's shape, not just its data.
Permissions are named `<resource>.<action>[.<qualifier>]` and are additive; there are no negative permissions.
A user cannot grant themselves a role they do not already have, and cannot remove their own admin role.
The last remaining admin cannot be demoted or suspended — the system must never become unadministrable.
Granting `admin` forces MFA enrolment on that account's next login.
A permission check failure is logged at `warn` with the permission name and raises an audit event.
Frontend permission data is advisory only; every server call re-checks.

errors.meaning: Authenticated but lacking the required permission
An actor tried to grant themselves a role
Would leave the system with no administrator

security: The guard is called in the **service** layer, not only in middleware — middleware protects a route, the guard protects an operation.
Ownership filtering is separate and mandatory; a `user` with `self.*` permissions must still only see their own rows.
Cached permissions have a short TTL so a revocation takes effect within 5 minutes; an immediate revocation also busts the key.

flows.title: Three-layer authorization
flows.description: Each layer catches a different mistake. Middleware catches a route wired to the wrong group; the guard catches a service method called from an unexpected path; the ownership filter catches the IDOR that the other two cannot see.
flows.mermaid:
flowchart TD A[Request] --> B[auth middleware
validates token → Actor in ctx] B --> C{Route group} C -->|/admin/*| D[require role=admin] C -->|/api/v1/*| E[authenticated] D --> F[Handler] E --> F F --> G[Service method] G --> H["rbac.Require(ctx, 'content.publish')"] H -->|denied| X[403 PERMISSION_DENIED
+ audit event] H -->|allowed| I[Repository query] I --> J["WHERE user_id = actor.UserID
(ownership — the real IDOR defence)"] J --> K[Result]

tasks.title: Add a permission
steps: Add the constant to `contract/permissions.go`.
Add the row in a migration and map it to the roles that should hold it.
Call `rbac.Require` in the service method that needs it.
Add `x-permission` to the operation in `openapi.yaml`.
Add a test asserting that a user without it receives 403 and that the denial is audited.
Update §5 of this file.

limitations: No resource-scoped permissions ("can edit *these* lessons"). If content ownership becomes a requirement, that is a new design, not a new row.
No time-bounded grants.
Permission changes take up to 5 minutes to propagate through the cache unless explicitly busted.
conventions: Never write a permission as a string literal at a call site — use the typed constant.
testFocus: Deny by default: an unguarded operation must fail a lint/test, not silently allow
A `user` calling any `/admin/*` route receives 403
Self-elevation and last-admin protection
Cache invalidation on role change takes effect
Every user-owned resource returns 404 (not 403) for another user's row

decisions.question: Casbin, OPA, or a table?
decisions.choice: A table plus a guard function
decisions.why: Two roles and ~40 permissions do not justify a policy engine, a policy language, and its evaluation semantics. Casbin becomes worth it at resource-scoped or hierarchical policies — recorded in ADR-0008 so the option is not forgotten

decisions.question: Roles in the JWT or looked up per request?
decisions.choice: Role in the token, permissions resolved from cache
decisions.why: The role is stable and small; permissions can change without reissuing tokens, and a 5-minute cache bounds staleness

todo.title: Phase 1
items: Roles, permissions, mappings seeded via migration
`Require`/`Can` guard with cached resolution
`/admin/*` route-group middleware
`GET /me/permissions`
Self-elevation and last-admin protections
A CI check that every non-public OpenAPI operation declares `x-permission`

future: Resource-scoped permissions if content ownership becomes a requirement
Temporary elevated access with automatic expiry
doNot: Do not add a third role without an ADR.
Do not rely on middleware alone — call the guard in the service.
Do not use the frontend's permission list as an authorization decision.
Do not implement ownership checks here; they belong in the owning module's query.

name: audit
purpose: Records what happened, who did it, and what changed — immutably. Two streams: an administrative audit trail (every state change made by an admin, and every significant change made by a user to their own data) and a security event stream (authentication anomalies, permission denials, suspicious patterns).
businessPurpose: When a learner says "my essay disappeared" or a regulator asks "who accessed this account", the answer must exist and must be trustworthy. Audit is also the raw material for the security dashboard.
responsibilities: Persisting audit entries with actor, action, target, before/after diff, IP, user agent, trace ID
Persisting security events with a severity
Enforcing append-only semantics
Retention and partition management
Query API for the admin UI, with filters and export
notResponsibilities: Deciding what is auditable — each module decides and emits
Application logs — those go to Loki; audit is durable business record, not telemetry
Alerting — Prometheus and Alertmanager do that

tables.name: audit_logs
tables.notes: Partitioned monthly on `created_at`, which the consumer takes from the emitting module's event so a redelivery lands in the same partition. `event_id` (the idempotency key, UNIQUE with `created_at`), `actor_id`, `actor_role`, `action`, `target_type`, `target_id`, `changed_fields` text[], `before`/`after`/`meta` jsonb, `ip_hash`, `trace_id`. No UPDATE or DELETE grant on this table, and none on its partitions.

tables.name: security_events
tables.notes: Partitioned monthly on `created_at` like the trail. `event_id`, `kind`, `severity`, `user_id`, `detail` jsonb, `ip_hash`, `trace_id`, `resolved_at`/`resolved_by`/`resolution_note`. Takes UPDATE so an event can be triaged, and still no DELETE.

indexes: `idx_audit_logs_actor_time` — the "what did this admin do" query
`idx_security_events_id` — resolving addresses an event by id alone, and the primary key leads with the partition key
All are declared on the parent, so every partition inherits them.

contract.name: audit.Recorder
contract.purpose: `Record(ctx, Entry)` — best effort from any module; it returns nothing, so it cannot fail the caller

contract.name: audit.SecurityRecorder
contract.purpose: `RecordSecurityEvent(ctx, SecurityEvent)` — the same, for the security stream

contract.name: audit.Entry
contract.purpose: `{Action, TargetType, TargetID, Before, After, ChangedFields, Meta}` — actor, client address and trace context come from `ctx`

contract.name: audit.PermissionRead / PermissionExport / PermissionManage
contract.purpose: The permission names the admin operations require, as plain strings — `audit` does not depend on `rbac`

consumes.name: user.* and rbac.*
consumes.reason: Persisted to `audit_logs`; `service.SubscribedTopics()` is the exact list

dependsWhy.job: Retention, partition rotation, and export run as scheduled jobs

rules: Audit entries are append-only. The application role holds no UPDATE or DELETE grant on `audit_logs`.
Recording an audit entry must never fail the business operation: it is written through the outbox in the same transaction where correctness matters, and best-effort otherwise.
Every admin action on another user's data is audited, including reads of personal data.
The `before`/`after` diff stores changed fields only, and redacts anything on the PII deny-list.
Retention is 2 years; partitions older than that are archived to object storage and detached.
Audit data survives account deletion in anonymised form — the record of an action must outlive the actor's profile.
Every entry carries the `trace_id`, so an audit row links directly to the full distributed trace.
security: Reading the audit trail is itself audited.
Exports are generated asynchronously and delivered by short-lived signed URL.
IP addresses are stored as a keyed HMAC-SHA256; the raw value is never persisted, and with no key configured nothing is stored at all.
`ip_hash` is never exposed on an API response.

flows.title: Recording an admin action
flows.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant AD as admin handler
    participant SV as content.Service
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant OB as outbox publisher
    participant AU as audit

    AD->>SV: PublishContent(ctx, id)
    SV->>DB: BEGIN
    SV->>DB: UPDATE content_versions SET status='published'
    SV->>DB: INSERT outbox(content.published, before, after)
    SV->>DB: COMMIT
    OB->>AU: deliver event
    AU->>DB: INSERT audit.audit_logs (actor, action, diff, trace_id)
    Note over AU,DB: at-least-once; the handler dedupes on event_id

tasks.title: Make a new action auditable
steps: Decide whether it must be transactional (money, permissions, publishing) or best-effort (a read).
Transactional: write an outbox event in the same transaction. Best-effort: call `audit.Recorder` directly.
Name the action `<module>.<verb>_<object>` and add it to the action catalogue in this file.
Ensure the diff excludes PII-deny-listed fields.
Add a test asserting the entry exists with the right actor and target.

limitations: There is no cryptographic chaining of entries; tamper-evidence relies on database grants and backups. Hash chaining is a candidate if a compliance requirement appears.
Diffs are field-level, not semantic — a reordered array shows as a full change.
`GET /admin/audit-logs/export` is specified but not implemented: an async export needs `storage` for the signed URL, and `audit` does not depend on it. See TODO.md.
Retention detaches an expired partition rather than archiving and dropping it, for the same reason. A detached partition keeps its rows and loses its grants.
Search is bounded to a 400-day window and defaults to 90 days, so a query can always be pruned to a fixed number of partitions. There is no way to ask for the whole table.
testFocus: The application role genuinely cannot UPDATE or DELETE audit rows — on the parent and on each partition
A partition created by the rotation job inherits the restricted grants rather than the schema defaults
Audit failure does not roll back the business operation
Duplicate event delivery produces exactly one row, including when the payload carries no occurred_at
PII redaction in diffs, asserted against the stored columns and not only the function
Partition rotation is idempotent, and retention detaches only fully expired months

decisions.question: Postgres or a log stream for audit?
decisions.why: Audit is queryable business record with retention and access-control requirements; Loki is optimised for cheap, short-lived telemetry and is not a system of record

decisions.question: Synchronous or asynchronous recording?
decisions.why: Permission and money changes go through the outbox so they cannot be lost; reads are best-effort so an audit outage cannot break browsing

todo.title: Phase 1
items: `audit_logs` and `security_events` with monthly partitions
`audit.Recorder` contract and outbox consumer
Append-only enforcement via database grants, proven by a test
Admin search UI endpoints with filters
Retention and partition-rotation jobs
PII redaction in diffs

future: Anomaly detection over the security event stream
Per-record access history shown to the user
doNot: Do not use audit as application logging — that is Loki.
Do not let an audit failure abort a business operation.
Do not store raw IP addresses or full user agents.
Do not grant UPDATE or DELETE on `audit_logs` to the application role, for any reason.

name: admin
purpose: The back-office surface. It owns almost no data of its own; it composes other modules' contracts into the screens an administrator needs: dashboards, user management, content moderation, feature flags, and operational tooling.
businessPurpose: Running the platform must not require database access. Every routine operational action — suspend a user, republish a lesson, re-run a failed grading job, flip a feature flag — has a screen, and every one of them is audited.
responsibilities: Admin dashboard aggregation across modules
User management screens (list, search, inspect, suspend, reinstate, impersonate)
Moderation queues (flagged content, reported names, flagged submissions)
Feature flag management
Operational actions: retry a job, replay a webhook, invalidate a cache key
System health summary for non-engineers
notResponsibilities: Any business rule — those live in the owning module; admin only calls contracts
Content authoring logic — that is `content`
Its own copies of other modules' data

tables.name: admin_actions
tables.purpose: Audit log of admin operations on accounts
tables.notes: `actor_id`, `target_id`, `action` (suspend/reinstate/revoke_sessions), `reason`, `occurred_at`. CHECK actor_id != target_id

tables.name: feature_flags
tables.notes: `key`, `enabled`, `rollout_percent`, `owner`, `expires_on`. Cached 30 s in-process.

tables.name: admin_notes
tables.purpose: Free-text notes attached to a user or content item
tables.notes: Visible to admins only; audited on create

tables.name: moderation_items
tables.notes: `kind`, `target_type`, `target_id`, `reason`, `status`, `assignee_id`

endpoints.notes: The search itself is not audited; opening one result is
Recorded as `admin.user_viewed`

endpoints.purpose: Suspend an account and end its sessions
endpoints.notes: Reason required; refused on the caller's own account

endpoints.purpose: Return a suspended account to active
endpoints.notes: Reason required; sessions are not restored
Reason required; status is unchanged
Unpaginated — the set is small by design
`owner` and a future `expires_on` are required
Visible within one 30 s cache generation
Evaluations of the key then return false
Audited; blocked for payment actions; a banner is shown throughout

contract.name: admin.FlagReader
contract.purpose: `IsEnabled(ctx, key, userID) bool` — used by every module that gates a feature

dependsWhy.auth: Session revocation and impersonation token issuance
dependsWhy.cache: Flag caching and operational cache invalidation

rules: Admin composes, it does not compute. Any rule an admin screen needs belongs in the owning module's service.
Every admin write action is audited with the acting admin's ID and, where the UI requires it, a stated reason.
Impersonation is time-boxed to 30 minutes, produces a visually distinct session, is fully audited, and is blocked for payment and deletion actions.
A feature flag defaults to disabled and carries an owner and an expiry date; expired flags are reported weekly.
Operational actions are idempotent — retrying a retry must not double-execute.
An admin cannot act on their own account through admin screens (suspension, role change) — that path goes through another admin.

errors.meaning: The attempted action is not permitted while impersonating
An admin may not administer their own account
A state-changing admin action was sent without a reason of at least 10 characters
The target user account does not exist
The requested feature flag does not exist
A feature flag with that key already exists

security: All `/admin/*` routes require the `admin` role at the route group and a specific permission at the service.
Admin accounts require MFA.
Reads of personal data are audited, not just writes.
Impersonation tokens carry an `act` claim so downstream audit entries record both identities.

flows.title: Impersonation
flows.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor AD as Admin
    participant A as admin
    participant AU as auth
    participant AD2 as audit

    AD->>A: POST /admin/impersonate/{user_id} { reason }
    A->>A: require permission user.impersonate
    A->>A: reject if target is an admin
    A->>AU: IssueImpersonationToken(admin_id, user_id, 30m)
    AU-->>A: token with act claim
    A->>AD2: audit(impersonation_started, reason)
    A-->>AD: token + banner flag
    Note over AD: every subsequent request records both identities
    Note over AD: payment, deletion and role changes are refused

tasks.title: Add an admin screen
steps: Identify which module owns the data and which contract methods you need. If a method does not exist, add it to that module's contract — do not query its tables.
Add the endpoint under `/api/v1/admin/` in `openapi.yaml` with an `x-permission`.
Implement a thin handler that composes contract calls.
Add the permission to `rbac` and map it to the admin role.
Audit any write.
Add the React page under `web/src/features/admin/`.

limitations: The dashboard aggregates synchronously across several modules; above a few thousand rows it will need a materialised read model.
Moderation is manual — there is no automated classification in Phase 2.
Feature flags are boolean plus a percentage; there is no targeting by attribute.
testFocus: A non-admin receives 403 on every `/admin/*` route
Impersonation cannot perform forbidden actions and expires on time
Self-administration is refused
Every write produces an audit entry with the correct actor
Flag changes propagate within the cache TTL

decisions.question: Separate admin service or the same binary?
decisions.why: A separate service would duplicate every contract call over the network for a handful of screens; the route group plus per-operation permissions gives the isolation that matters

decisions.question: Does admin own data?
decisions.choice: Only flags, notes and the moderation queue
decisions.why: Anything else would duplicate another module's state and drift from it

decisions.question: Does user erasure purge `core.admin_actions`?
decisions.why: The rows record who acted on whom and why. Like `audit`, this is an accountability log that must outlive the account it describes, or an administrator could erase the evidence of their own action by deleting the target. The erasure completeness check excludes it by name for this reason — see `internal/modules/user/job/erasure_checker.go`

Moderation queue with assignment and resolution

Impersonation with all its guards

doNot: Do not query another module's tables from admin — call its contract.
Do not implement business rules here.
Do not add an admin action without a permission and an audit entry.
Do not allow impersonation of another admin.

name: notification
purpose: Turns domain events into messages a learner actually sees: in-app notifications, push notifications and emails. Owns delivery preferences, quiet hours, digesting, and deduplication.
businessPurpose: Retention in a learning product depends on timely, welcome nudges — a due-review reminder, a graded essay, a streak about to break. The same mechanism becomes an annoyance if it is noisy, badly timed, or ignores preferences, so restraint is a first-class requirement.
responsibilities: Notification templates and rendering per channel and locale
Delivery preferences per category and channel
Quiet hours in the learner's own timezone
Digesting: collapsing many events into one message
Deduplication and rate limiting per user
In-app inbox: list, mark read, unread count
Push device registration and token lifecycle
notResponsibilities: Sending the email — `platform/mailer` does the transport
Deciding that something happened — modules publish events

dependsWhy.cache: Unread counts, dedupe keys, per-user rate limits

rules: A notification is never sent for a category the user has disabled, on a channel they have disabled.
Quiet hours are evaluated in the learner's own timezone; a message that would land inside them is deferred to the next allowed slot, not dropped — unless it is a security notice, which always sends.
Security notices (password changed, new device, session revoked) ignore preferences and quiet hours.
Deduplication: the same `dedupe_key` within its window produces exactly one message.
No more than one push and three emails per user per day, excluding security notices.
Related events within a digest window collapse into one message ("3 essays graded") rather than three.
Delivery is at-least-once from the outbox; the dispatcher is idempotent on `event_id`.
A push token that fails twice with a permanent error is deleted.
Every message includes a working unsubscribe or preferences link, except security notices.

errors.meaning: Too many registered push devices
Window is malformed or spans more than 12 hours

flows.title: Event to delivered notification
flows.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant W as writing
    participant OB as outbox
    participant N as notification
    participant C as Redis
    participant J as job
    participant M as mailer
    actor U as User

    W->>OB: writing.graded (in the grading transaction)
    OB->>N: deliver event
    N->>N: load preferences + timezone
    alt category disabled on every channel
        N->>N: drop, record reason
    else
        N->>C: check dedupe key
        alt duplicate
            N->>N: suppress
        else
            N->>N: INSERT notifications (in-app is always written)
            N->>C: bust unread count
            alt inside quiet hours
                N->>J: schedule for the next allowed slot
            else
                N->>J: enqueue push + email now
                J->>M: render + send
                M-->>U: email
            end
        end
    end

tasks.title: Add a notification category
steps: Add the category constant and its default channel settings.
Write templates for every channel and every supported locale.
Subscribe to the triggering event, or call `Notify` directly for a non-event trigger.
Choose a dedupe key and window, and decide whether it participates in a digest.
Add it to the preferences UI.
Test: disabled preference suppresses it; quiet hours defer it; duplicates collapse.

limitations: Web push only — no native mobile push until there is a mobile app.
Digest windows are fixed per category rather than learned from behaviour.
Send-time optimisation is a fixed heuristic (the learner's usual study hour), not a model.
testFocus: Preference matrix: every category × channel combination behaves
Quiet hours across timezone boundaries and DST transitions
Deduplication under concurrent event delivery
Digest collapsing
Security notices bypass preferences and quiet hours
Idempotency on redelivered events

decisions.question: One notification module or per-channel modules?
decisions.why: Preferences, quiet hours, dedupe and digesting are channel-independent policy; splitting by channel would triplicate the policy and let the three copies diverge

decisions.question: Write in-app notifications even when other channels are disabled?
decisions.why: The inbox is the durable record; suppressing it would lose information the learner may want later

doNot: Do not send a notification synchronously inside a request — enqueue it.
Do not bypass preference checks for anything except a genuine security notice.
Do not put personal content (essay text, scores) in a push payload — link to the app.
Do not add a category without templates for every supported locale.
